deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a fair-copy page of lecture notes on ancient Greek history, continuing from the previous page (Cimon, the Eurymedon victory) and running into the next (Pericles, Tanagra, the five-year truce). The page covers six points.
(1) Cimon's activity on the Thracian Chersonese, dated 468 in the margin.
(2) Punitive expeditions against Delian League allies who refused to pay tribute. The margin gives examples: Carystus, Euboea 467; Naxos 466; Thasos 465–463.
(3) The great earthquake at Sparta (margin 'a. 465'). It led to the Helot revolt, which the Messenians joined. The revolt lasted 10 years with changing fortunes; the rebels held Ithome. The margin notes that this is therefore called the 3rd Messenian War.
(4) On Cimon's initiative Athens offered Sparta help, which was rejected. Cimon was consequently banished (margin 461).
(5) Pericles, son of Xanthippus, from one of the first and richest families, made himself head of the democrats in opposition to the aristocrat Cimon. He had influence from 469, held his position as demagogue for 40 years, and was wealthy and highly educated.
(6) The text breaks off mid-sentence and continues on the next page ('...unter die durch Kunst gebildeter Redner').
The hand, the content and the layout (chronological margin dates, underlined key names such as Ithome and Pericles) indicate student notes from a university history lecture. Göttingen ancient-history lectures in the Heeren tradition are a plausible source, but this is my conjecture. Nothing on the page is a Gauss research note, and there is no derivation to reconstruct.
errors: Historical dating differs slightly from modern consensus. The Spartan earthquake is usually dated 464 BC, not 465. Carystus is usually put c. 472 and Naxos c. 470/469, not 467/466. Ithome was in fact the stronghold of the rebels. These are possible inaccuracies in the lecture or the notes, not mathematical errors.
'Xantippus' is the period spelling of Xanthippus.
The statement that Pericles held his position for 40 years (from 469) is the traditional ancient rhetoric (cf. Plutarch). Modern scholarship would date his dominance later, c. 461/443–429.
